How an Indiana tax bill is calculated

The sequence starts at gross assessed value. Deductions reduce it to net assessed value, the local rate multiplies the result, and credits plus a cap finish the job. DLGF, the state's local government finance agency, walks through the order on its Tax Bill 101 page.

  • Deductions, including the homestead and mortgage deductions, are subtracted first.
  • All parcels inside one taxing district share a rate assembled from county, city, school, township and library levies.
  • Percentage credits follow, and local option income tax revenue pays for some of them.
  • If the bill still exceeds the cap, a circuit breaker credit trims it down.
  • Special assessments, such as ditch charges, go on last.

The cap leaves the rate alone. Local budgets set the rate, and the cap only limits what a particular owner pays against the property's gross assessed value.

Property tax caps

A home's tax is limited to 1 percent of gross assessed value, and other property classes have higher limits. The caps were added to Article 10, Section 1 of the state constitution by voters in November 2010 and have governed bills since 2010.

Property classCap on gross assessed value
Homestead (must receive the standard deduction)1%
Other residential, long-term care, agricultural land2%
Nonresidential and personal property3%

Voter-approved school and public safety levies, and some capital project levies, sit outside the cap in most counties. That explains an adjustment line on some statements. Beginning with Pay 2025, residential yard structures count as residential property under the 2 percent cap.

Apartments, vacation homes and other non-homestead residential property sit under the 2 percent cap. A house an heir turns into a rental belongs to that group as well.

Due dates and late penalties

IC 6-1.1-22-9 splits each year's tax into two equal payments made the year after assessment, on May 10 and November 10. A bill for 2025 property is a 2026 payment, which DLGF labels 2025 Pay 2026. When a date falls on a weekend or holiday, payment moves to the next business day.

Lateness is priced in two tiers. Pay within 30 days after the due date and the parcel has no earlier delinquency, and the penalty is 5 percent. In every other case it is 10 percent. Later on, another 10 percent attaches to unpaid principal the day after each installment date.

Two details are useful at closing:

  • A county council may require a bill under $25 to be paid in a single May installment.
  • After an appeal changes levies, a reconciling statement shows the balance still owed, payable by November 10 unless the county picks other dates.

Since Indiana bills in arrears, the title company prorates the tax between buyer and seller at the closing table.

The 2025 law and the homestead deduction

Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025 phases out the flat homestead deduction and shifts part of the relief to a percentage deduction. The flat amount runs $48,000 for 2025, $40,000 for 2026, $30,000 for 2027, $20,000 for 2028, $10,000 for 2029 and $0 from 2030. The percentage deduction, applied to taxes payable, is 40 percent for 2026, then 46, 52, 57 and 62 percent for 2027 through 2030, and 66.7 percent for 2031 onward.

Lower-value homes may see double-digit bill increases while expensive homes may see small decreases. The two deductions break even at a $102,740 home. Starting in 2026, a new supplemental credit of 10 percent, up to $300, applies after the caps.

Other changes touch sellers and heirs. Over 65 relief is now a credit instead of a deduction, and from January 1, 2026 the claimant has to live on the property. A service-connected disability rating of at least 10 percent earns a $350 credit, and the same rating at age 62 or older earns a $250 credit. Anyone who holds on to a homestead deduction after losing eligibility owes the back taxes and a 10 percent civil penalty, so look hard at any empty house whose owner moved to care or died.

How assessments are set and adjusted

Each year, assessors revise real property values with mass appraisal methods that follow DLGF rules, and they must tell the owner when a revision raises the assessment. IC 6-1.1-4-4.5 governs those years between general reassessments, linking each adjustment to estimated true tax value on the assessment date that sets the taxes payable.

The Form 11 notice of assessment starts the appeal clock. An appeal moves from Form 130 to the county assessment board and then to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131. Transfer prices reported on the sales disclosure form at closing reach the state and county and feed the yearly adjustments. Ask the county assessor what the appeal deadline is this year.

What happens when taxes go unpaid?

If you fall behind, the county can put the parcel on its tax sale list, and whoever wins the bid receives a certificate instead of the house. IC 6-1.1-24-1 makes real property eligible once taxes from the prior year's spring installment or earlier are delinquent and the total owed, penalties and fees included, is above $25. After January 1 of the sale year, and within 51 days after the first payment due date, the county treasurer certifies the list.

Bidding opens at a minimum bid built from these pieces:

  • overdue taxes and special assessments;
  • current-year taxes and assessments, even before they turn delinquent;
  • the penalties on those overdue amounts;
  • what the county spent on the sale, plus any costs left unpaid from an earlier sale;
  • other reasonable collection costs such as a title search and attorney's fees.

A parcel on the vacant and abandoned list may go for less, and its owner has no redemption right afterward.

Owners of other parcels get time to buy the property back. Under IC 6-1.1-25-4 the window is one year from the sale, shortened to 120 days when a qualified purchasing agency bought. The price is 110 percent of the minimum bid if paid within six months and 115 percent after six months, plus interest on any excess bid, taxes the buyer paid and certified costs. The treasurer and owner may agree to a payment plan that stretches the window, usually to one year after the agreement.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing taxes does not block a sale, since the payoff is handled at closing. Selling during the redemption window adds hurdles. IC 32-21-8-7 bars the county auditor from endorsing the deed until the buyer pays the treasurer the full redemption amount and hands the auditor written proof. A deed not recorded by the end of the window is void.

If nobody redeems after a tax sale, the former owner can still file a verified claim on the surplus fund. Money unclaimed three years after receipt goes to the county general fund.

Sellers who fall behind usually want three things in order: the exact payoff, a closing date that falls before the next installment, and proof that nothing else is recorded against the parcel. Asking the treasurer's office early for a written payoff, and the auditor's office for the endorsement timeline, keeps a closing from slipping over a missing stamp.

In an ordinary sale with back taxes, the title company asks the treasurer for a payoff figure and deducts it from the seller's proceeds. A cash buyer will typically take the house as is, so a tax debt alone need not end the deal.

What sellers see on a 2026 tax statement

The 2026 statement adds credit lines for the Over 65 Credit, the Blind/Disabled Credit, the Supplemental Homestead Credit and the County Option Homestead Relief Credit. Each tax rate is split into debt and non-debt parts, and a percentage of total liability column is new.

Every taxpayer gets a bill, even with a zero balance, and escrowed accounts may carry an In Escrow or For Informational Purposes Only watermark.

Frequently asked questions

When do Indiana property taxes come due?

Payments are split into two equal installments on May 10 and November 10 of the year following assessment. A weekend or holiday pushes the deadline to the next business day.

How high can the tax on a home go?

A homestead with the standard deduction is limited to 1 percent of gross assessed value. Other residential and agricultural land is limited to 2 percent, and nonresidential and personal property to 3 percent.

What does a late payment cost?

Paying within 30 days after the due date on a parcel with a clean record costs 5 percent. Otherwise the penalty is 10 percent, and another 10 percent can be added to unpaid tax in later years.

How long can I redeem a parcel after a tax sale?

One year, or 120 days if a qualified purchasing agency bought it. The price is 110 percent of the minimum bid in the first six months and 115 percent afterward, plus the other statutory amounts. Vacant and abandoned parcels have no redemption right.

Can I sell with back property taxes owed?

Yes. The title company gets a payoff from the county treasurer and pays it from your proceeds. If the parcel already sold at a tax sale, the redemption amount must be paid before the auditor endorses the deed.

The standard homestead deduction and its phase-out

Indiana's standard homestead deduction is shrinking each year until it reaches zero, so what you receive depends on the assessment year. Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025 swapped the old formula, the lesser of 60 percent of assessed value or $48,000, for a fixed schedule that applies back to January 1, 2025.

Assessment dateStandard deduction
Before Jan. 1, 2025Lesser of 60% of assessed value or $48,000
2025$48,000
2026$40,000
2027$30,000
2028$20,000
2029$10,000
2030 and later$0

A smaller standard deduction does not mean relief vanishes. The state added a supplemental deduction and a credit to carry more of the load.

Supplemental deduction and homestead credit

The supplemental deduction takes a percentage of whatever value remains after the standard deduction, and that percentage climbs each year. It applies to taxes first due and payable after December 31, 2025, and it cannot exceed 75 percent of the property's gross assessed value.

  • 2026 taxes: 40 percent
  • 2027: 46 percent
  • 2028: 52 percent
  • 2029: 57 percent
  • 2030: 62 percent
  • 2031 and later: 66.7 percent

Anyone who receives the standard deduction also gets a supplemental homestead credit. It equals the lesser of 10 percent of the homestead's tax liability or $300, needs no application, and leaves out taxes voters approved in a referendum. For 2026 it is applied after the property tax cap credit and before the over 65 circuit breaker credit.

Who qualifies for the deduction?

The person claiming it must live in the property as a principal residence in Indiana and hold an interest in it on the assessment date. IC 6-1.1-12-37 allows that interest to take several forms:

  • Ownership by the individual.
  • A recorded contract that makes the buyer responsible for the property taxes and obligates the owner to convey title when the contract is complete.
  • Occupancy as a tenant-stockholder of a cooperative housing corporation.
  • A home held in a trust, when the occupant is a person described in section 17.9, such as someone with a beneficial interest in the trust.

The contract purchaser line is worth a look for anyone who sold on a land contract. When the contract is recorded and the buyer pays the taxes, the buyer may claim the deduction while the seller still holds title.

House Enrolled Act 1210 now writes a definition into the statute: an individual's true, fixed, permanent home to which the individual intends to return after an absence.

What counts as the homestead

The deduction covers one house and one garage, plus up to one acre immediately around the dwelling. It can also reach decks, patios, gazebos, pools, one additional yard structure and one additional residential building that is not an investment or rental property. Land and buildings beyond that are ordinary residential property, capped at 2 percent instead of 1 percent. In general a person cannot hold the deduction on two properties in the same year.

How to apply

You apply by filing a certified statement with the county auditor. The first filing is normally the only one, because reapplication is needed only if the property is sold or the title changes. Call the county auditor for the current filing deadline before you file.

  • The Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF) offers a Homestead Deduction Form and a separate Change of Use form for owners whose use of the property changes.
  • The statement lists the applicant and spouse by name, with the last five digits of each Social Security number or an allowed substitute.
  • The sales disclosure form filed when a house sells can double as an application for deductions such as the homestead deduction, so a buyer can apply on that form.

Credits that need their own application are due by January 15, so ask the auditor which forms apply to you.

When you sell the house

The deduction does not move to the buyer on its own. Because reapplication is needed when a property is sold or the title changes, the new owner must file a fresh statement, and until then the property may be billed without the benefit.

That matters because the 1 percent circuit breaker cap applies only to homestead property that receives the standard deduction. A house with no deduction loses the 1 percent cap and falls under the higher limit.

Duties for a seller who moved out

A person who stops being eligible must tell the auditor within 60 days. An owner who keeps claiming the deduction anyway is liable for the extra tax plus a civil penalty of 10 percent of the additional taxes. The statute now says shall, where it once said may.

The auditor has a firm duty as well. If a property was ineligible in any year within three years of the tax due date, the auditor shall send a notice of taxes, interest and penalties. The notice adds a 10 percent penalty on the total bill calculated as if the deduction had never applied. A vacant inherited house that still carries a deceased owner's deduction deserves a call to the auditor before you list.

Other credits and deductions that follow the owner

Several senior, disability and military-service benefits changed under the 2025 and 2026 laws. Most are credits with a separate application. They stack with each other and with the homestead deduction.

  • Over 65 credit: up to $150. Age 65 by Dec. 31 of the prior year; adjusted gross income of $60,000 (single) or $70,000 (joint).
  • Over 65 circuit breaker credit: varies by bill. Same income limits, up from $30,000 and $40,000, and the $240,000 value limit is removed.
  • Blind or disabled credit: up to $125. No income limit; principal residence.
  • Disabled veteran credit, age 62 and up: $250, with a disability of 10% or more.
  • Service-connected veteran credit: $350, with a disability of 10% or more and war-time service.
  • Totally disabled veteran deduction: 100% of assessed value, for a principal residence with one year of Indiana residency.

An over 65 claimant must now live on the property, though a nursing home or hospital stay does not disqualify. A credit larger than the year's tax liability is neither carried forward nor refunded.

Rental owners get relief too. Residential, long-term care and agricultural property in the 2 percent class receives a deduction applied automatically, set at 6 percent of assessed value for the 2025 assessment and rising to 33.4 percent from the 2030 assessment onward.

Protection from creditors is a separate rule

Indiana Code 34-55-10-2(c)(1) exempts real estate or personal property used as the debtor's or a dependent's residence from creditors, up to a dollar limit set by the statute.

Joint debtors can each use the exemption for property held as tenants by the entirety. Under subsection (c)(5), any interest a debtor has in entireties property is exempt, except for a debt the debtor and the debtor's spouse owe together. The dollar amounts are adjusted over time, so confirm the present figure with an Indiana attorney before a sale that involves a judgment or bankruptcy.

This protection does nothing for a property tax bill, and the tax deduction does not shield a house from a judgment.

Frequently asked questions

Does the homestead deduction go away when I sell my Indiana house?

It ends for you as the owner. Reapplication is needed when a property is sold or the title changes, so the buyer files their own statement with the county auditor if they will live there.

What is the Indiana homestead deduction in 2026?

The standard deduction is $40,000 for the 2026 assessment date, down from $48,000 for 2025. A supplemental deduction of 40 percent of the remaining value applies to 2026 taxes, capped at 75 percent of gross assessed value.

When is the deadline to file for the homestead deduction?

Call your county auditor for the date they enforce. Credits that need their own application are due by January 15.

Can I claim the deduction on a house I am buying on a land contract?

Possibly. A contract purchaser can qualify when the contract is recorded, makes the buyer responsible for the property taxes and obligates the owner to convey title when the contract is complete. The house must also be the buyer's principal residence.

What happens if I keep the deduction after I move out?

You must notify the county auditor within 60 days of becoming ineligible. If you do not, you owe the additional taxes plus a 10 percent civil penalty on the extra tax, and the auditor must send a notice for any ineligible year within three years of the due date.

Indiana inheritance tax is gone

Indiana has no inheritance tax today. It reached only people who died on or before December 31, 2012, and the legislature repealed it in 2013. A family selling a Hoosier house after a death owes the state nothing simply because the owner passed away.

The state stopped accepting returns, too. Nobody should prepare or file an Indiana inheritance tax return for a resident or nonresident, and the old forms are retired. Questions go to the Inheritance Tax Division at 317-232-2154, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Eastern.

Heirs sometimes worry that a recorded deed will trigger a state filing. For a house passing from an estate to a buyer or to the heirs, no Indiana inheritance tax step is needed.

A title company can still ask what applies to a given deed. For a particular gain, call a tax professional or an attorney.

Old inheritance tax wording in the Indiana Code

Section 6-4.1-4-0.5 still refers to the exemptions in repealed chapter 6-4.1-3. It appears in the passage allowing an affidavit that says no tax is due.

That section also says a terminated lien can reattach if the state wins an order finding inheritance tax owed. When the death in your family was decades ago, a title search may surface this language, and an attorney can say whether it matters for your file.

Federal estate tax

The IRS runs a separate estate tax, and it touches only very large estates. A return is required when the gross estate, added to adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, exceeds the filing threshold for the year of death. A person who died in 2025 is measured against the 2025 number even if the house closes in 2026.

Since 2011, the estate of a person survived by a spouse can pass any unused exemption to that spouse. The estate makes this election on a timely filed estate tax return.

Indiana inheritance taxRepealed in 2013; applied to deaths through December 31, 2012
Indiana inheritance tax returnsNot filed; forms retired
Federal estate tax filing threshold, 2025$13,990,000
Federal estate tax filing threshold, 2026$15,000,000

Tax on an heir's sale of the house

Once an heir sells, any taxable gain is counted from the house's worth at the owner's death. What the original owner paid does not matter. The personal representative can instead pick the alternate valuation date, and then the basis is the value on that date.

Gifts carve out an exception. Suppose you or your spouse gave appreciated property to the decedent in the final year of life. Your basis is then the decedent's adjusted basis from just before death.

  • Request the appraisal or the estate's valuation of the house.
  • Save receipts for repairs and carrying costs paid after the death.
  • Remember that Indiana applies its flat individual rate to income reported on the federal return. The Indiana capital gains page shows how.

When can heirs skip full probate?

A small estate can be wrapped up without notifying creditors in some cases. Under section 29-1-8-3, that works for deaths after June 30, 2022 when the gross probate estate, net of liens and encumbrances, stays within $100,000 plus administration costs and reasonable funeral expenses. A fiduciary handles the distribution.

Where land is involved, an affidavit goes on record with the recorder of the county that holds the parcel. Every affidavit needs these items:

  • The legal description of the property
  • The threshold amount in effect on the date of death
  • Each entitled person's name and the share that person takes, divided or undivided
  • A statement explaining how each share was worked out

Personal property follows a different rule. Section 29-1-8-1 allows distributees to collect it by affidavit 45 days after death, provided nobody has applied for a personal representative anywhere. Bank funds, vehicles and securities fit here. Land does not.

Unsupervised administration and selling the house

Bigger estates are run by a personal representative. Under Indiana Code 29-1-7.5-1, the heirs at law, the legatees and devisees, or the representative may ask the court for permission to administer without supervision.

A notice comes next. The clerk issues it, and the petitioner serves the known creditors. Before a listing goes live, check the representative's authority to sell real estate with a probate attorney or with the clerk where the case was filed.

Practice differs from county to county among Indiana's 92 counties. Howard County has five courts, a Circuit Court and Superior Courts I through IV, so ask the clerk which court takes your filing.

Bills that keep coming while an estate owns the house

Property tax is the carrying cost with a hard calendar, and it arrives whether or not the owner is alive. Installments are due in May and November. Pay within 30 days after the due date on a parcel with no back taxes and the charge is 5 percent. Pay later and it grows to 10 percent of the unpaid tax.

Because Indiana bills a year behind, a spring bill after a death often reflects the previous year's ownership. A homestead deduction is renewed only when the property is sold, the title changes or a contract is paid off. Heirs who take title should check the deduction status with their county auditor, such as the Howard County Auditor.

Closing day itself is straightforward once the paperwork is right. The title company asks for proof of who may sign, orders the payoff of any tax owed on the parcel and records the deed with the county. Whatever remains goes to the estate or to the heirs under the will or the intestacy shares.

Insurance and utilities also continue. An empty house with a lapsed policy is a risk the estate carries, so heirs who plan to sell should confirm coverage while the house sits.

Paperwork to gather before listing

A complete file speeds up every step. Heirs usually need:

  • A certified death certificate, plus the will if one exists
  • Court letters, or the recorded affidavit if the estate qualifies
  • The deed, the parcel number and the newest property tax bill
  • The date-of-death value, which becomes the starting basis
  • A list of everyone entitled to a share, because the affidavit names each person and each share

Talk to an Indiana probate attorney before anyone signs a deed, since the correct route turns on the estate's size and who holds legal authority. After that authority is shown to the title company, a cash buyer can often close without a financing delay. That spares heirs months of taxes and insurance on a house nobody lives in.

Frequently asked questions

Does Indiana have an estate tax?

Indiana's old inheritance tax was repealed in 2013 and applied to deaths through December 31, 2012. The federal estate tax is a separate matter, with a 2026 filing threshold of $15,000,000.

Do heirs owe Indiana inheritance tax on a house?

No. Indiana no longer takes inheritance tax returns, and the forms are retired.

Does an inherited house get a stepped-up basis?

In general, yes. Basis is the fair market value at death, or the alternate valuation date if the personal representative elects it. A gift to the decedent within one year before death is the exception.

How big can an estate be and still use the small estate process?

For deaths after June 30, 2022, the cap is $100,000 of gross probate estate after liens and encumbrances, plus administration costs and reasonable funeral expenses. For real property, the affidavit is recorded with the county recorder.

Do property taxes stop when the owner dies?

No. Bills continue each May and November, and late payment brings a 5 percent charge and then a 10 percent charge.

How an eviction starts

Every Indiana eviction opens with written notice, and the length of that notice depends on the reason. When rent is unpaid, Indiana Code 32-31-1-6 lets a landlord end the lease with at least ten days' notice unless the parties agreed to something else. If the tenant pays all the rent before the ten days run out, the termination stops.

Legal aid groups describe the same ten-day notice as the usual first step for nonpayment or another lease violation. A landlord cannot end the lease if the rent comes in during those days.

Notices under the first seven sections of the chapter can be served three ways under section 32-31-1-9:

  • Hand it to the tenant directly
  • Give it to a person living at the property and explain what it says, if the tenant cannot be found
  • Attach a copy to a conspicuous spot on the premises when no one is home

Which notice fits which tenancy?

Notice depends on the kind of tenancy, and a few situations call for none. Section 32-31-1-8 lists six of them, among them a lease for a set period, a contract that states its end date, a tenant at will who commits waste and a tenant at sufferance.

SituationNotice required
Rent unpaidAt least 10 days; cured if the tenant pays in full first
Tenant at will commits waste, or tenant at sufferanceNone
Fixed term or stated end dateNone
No landlord-tenant relationshipNone

Sections 32-31-1-1 through 1-5 deal separately with estates at will and year-to-year tenancies and how notice ends them. Start with your lease, because its term decides which rule governs.

What happens in court

Most Indiana eviction cases unfold in two stages. A possession hearing comes first, and a damages hearing may follow later. At the possession hearing the judge decides who gets the unit under the lease. The damages hearing settles whether either side owes money for rent, utilities or repairs.

Two possession outcomes are common:

  • Final possession, the usual result for unpaid rent, with a move-out date typically two to three weeks away
  • Immediate possession, where the landlord pays money into court in case the tenant later wins, and the tenant can post the same amount to stay until the damages hearing

Small claims court caps awards at $10,000, so a tenant who skips the damages hearing can face a judgment up to that amount. A party who does not appear can lose by default, and a missed hearing can block a tenant from sealing an old eviction later.

Chapter 32-31-6 also covers emergency possessory orders, with sections on small claims jurisdiction, emergency hearings, waste and criminal activity.

Locks, utilities and entry

A landlord cannot change the locks to force a tenant out. Section 32-31-5-6 says a landlord may not deny or interfere with access to or possession of the dwelling without a court order. That covers changing locks and removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances.

The same section bars cutting or reducing electricity, gas, water or other essential services. The exceptions are an emergency, good faith repairs and necessary construction. A landlord must give reasonable written or oral notice before coming in and may enter only at reasonable times. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for inspections, repairs or showings.

That last item matters to an owner who wants to sell, since showings are one of the listed reasons for entry. The section does not apply to a unit that has been truly abandoned, meaning the tenant failed to pay or offer rent and a reasonable person would conclude possession was given up.

Does selling a rented house cancel the lease?

No. Under section 32-31-1-10, a landlord's conveyance of the property or any interest in it is valid without the tenant's attornment. If the tenant pays rent to the old landlord before learning about the conveyance, that payment holds up against the new owner.

Deposits have their own chapter. Section 32-31-3-19, titled for the sale of property and liability for deposits, covers how a deposit passes at closing, so read it or ask an attorney. Under section 32-31-3-12, the landlord owes an itemized written notice and the deposit balance within 45 days after the rental agreement ends. No liability attaches until the tenant supplies a written mailing address.

Allowed deductions are unpaid rent, damage caused by a violation of law or the lease, and unpaid utility or sewer charges the lease puts on the tenant. A landlord who does not comply can owe the full deposit plus reasonable attorney's fees.

Local rules

Indiana cities mostly cannot add their own landlord rules. Section 32-31-1-20 bars local governments from controlling rents on private property or regulating the landlord-tenant relationship without state authorization. Barred topics include tenant screening, security deposits, rental applications, lease terms, required disclosures, the rights of parties under a lease and landlord fees.

A local rule that crosses the line is void and unenforceable. The exception covers private property receiving government funds or benefits to offer reduced rents to low or moderate income tenants.

A landlord selling in Kokomo or Fort Wayne therefore follows the state code and the county court, not a city rent ordinance.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Indiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If the tenant dies or cannot be found

When a sole occupant dies, section 32-31-1-23 sets up a tenant's representative to collect belongings and the deposit. The representative is picked in order: a person the tenant named in writing to the landlord or in the lease, then an attorney-in-fact, a guardian, an heir, or someone a probate court appoints.

The landlord must give the representative access at a reasonable time to remove personal property, may require an inventory, and must pay the deposit and unearned rent. A landlord who follows the section is protected from liability, and a willful violation exposes the landlord to actual damages. The same steps apply to an absent, apparently incapacitated sole occupant.

Preparing a tenant-occupied house for sale

Collect the tenant paperwork before a buyer asks for it:

  • The lease and any renewal, so the tenancy type and term are clear
  • A rent ledger showing what was paid and when
  • Any notice you served, with proof of how and when it was delivered
  • The security deposit amount, and the tenant's written mailing address if you have one
  • Repair requests and your responses, since a recent repair request or code enforcement call is something a tenant may raise in court
  • Court papers if a case is already filed, including hearing dates

If you and the tenant can agree on a move-out date, you avoid a hearing entirely. An owner who prefers to sell rather than continue a case can still do so, and an attorney can confirm how a pending court order affects timing. Buyers paying cash often accept a house with a tenant or a pending case as is, which lets an owner stop managing the dispute.

Frequently asked questions

How much notice does an Indiana landlord give for unpaid rent?

At least ten days under Indiana Code 32-31-1-6. If the tenant pays all of the rent before the notice runs out, the lease cannot be ended for that default.

How long does a tenant have to move after a judgment?

A final possession judgment typically sets a move-out date two to three weeks away. The exact date comes from the court's order in your case.

Can a landlord lock a tenant out?

No. Section 32-31-5-6 bars a landlord from denying or interfering with access or possession without a court order, including by changing locks or cutting off essential utilities.

Does the tenant have to leave if I sell the house?

Not automatically. Under section 32-31-1-10 the sale is valid without the tenant's attornment, so the lease continues until it ends by its own terms or by proper notice.

When must a landlord return a security deposit?

Within 45 days after the rental agreement ends, with an itemized written notice of deductions, under section 32-31-3-12. The landlord has no liability until the tenant gives a written mailing address.

What a quitclaim deed transfers

Whatever the grantor owns, a quitclaim hands over, and nothing more. The statute (IC 32-17-2-2) describes the effect as conveying the estate the grantor could convey by a deed of bargain and sale. The grantee therefore stands exactly where the grantor stood.

Indiana also provides a short form in IC 32-21-1-15. A conveyance that says in substance 'A.B. quitclaims to C.D.' works if it describes the property, states the price after the words 'for the sum of,' and carries a signature, a seal and an acknowledgment. The result is a valid quitclaim for the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns.

No promise about title appears anywhere in that form. Someone who accepts a quitclaim cannot sue on deed covenants later, and that gap matters most when the buyer is paying money.

What the deed must include to be recorded

A signature alone will not get a deed accepted. The recorder also looks for a notarial act, two mailing addresses, a preparer statement and a redaction affirmation about Social Security numbers. Each comes from a specific code section.

  • Acknowledgment or proof. IC 32-21-2-3 calls for a notarial officer's acknowledgment or a proof, and Indiana allows remote notarization under the cited sections.
  • Addresses. The deed states the mailing address for tax statements and the grantee's mailing address. The grantee's address must be a street or rural route address, and the statement goes at the end of the deed beside the preparer statements.
  • Prepared by. IC 36-2-11-15 wants the preparer's name printed, typed, stamped or signed at the end, for example 'This instrument was prepared by' and the name.
  • Redaction. The preparer affirms under penalties of perjury that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers, unless a law requires them.
  • Names. Each signer's name is printed under the signature and kept identical throughout, including the notary block.
  • Format. Margins are at least 2 inches top and bottom on the first and last pages, paper is white and no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, and bound or continuous-form pages are refused.

A deed signed outside Indiana is treated differently on one point: instruments executed or acknowledged outside the state are exempt from the preparer statement rule, and a foreign-language document needs an English translation.

Recording costs

The base county recorder fee for an ordinary deed is $25 under IC 36-2-7-10, and the sales disclosure filing adds $20 when it applies. Counties may add small charges by ordinance, so the recorder's current schedule controls.

Recording itemAmount
Recording a deed (standard pages)$25 flat
Oversized pages (over 8.5 by 14 inches)$25 first page, $5 each additional
Copy of a recorded page$1 per page up to 11 by 17 inches
Certifying a document$5
Sales disclosure form fee$20, paid to the county auditor
Affordable housing fund (some counties)$10 per document

If you are budgeting for a family transfer, ask the county auditor whether the endorsement carries a charge, and expect a notary fee on top.

Auditor endorsement and the sales disclosure form

Two offices handle a deed before it is filed: the county auditor, then the recorder. Many transfers need a sales disclosure form as well. Under IC 36-2-11-14, the recorder can record a land conveyance only after the auditor has endorsed it 'duly entered for taxation subject to final acceptance for transfer,' 'not taxable,' or 'duly entered for taxation.'

The disclosure rules are narrower. A form is required whenever a real property interest moves for valuable consideration in a deed, contract, judgment or similar document. Exempt from the form altogether are quitclaim deeds that do not serve as a source of title, gifts with no valuable consideration, mortgages and transfers to a government unit. Foreclosure, divorce, court-ordered, condemnation and probate transfers need the form but owe no fee.

The transferor and the transferee sign the form, the county assessor reviews and stamps it, and it then goes to the auditor. The auditor may not accept a conveyance when the form is missing, incomplete or unstamped. Each parcel needs its own form, although one form can cover contiguous parcels in the same taxing district under a single deed.

Transfer on death deed versus quitclaim

A transfer on death deed is a different tool. It names who receives the house after the owner dies, and it follows its own rules. IC 32-17-14-11 requires the deed to be on record with the county recorder before death. No consideration, no delivery and no auditor endorsement is needed.

How the owner holds title changes the outcome. On tenancy by the entirety property the deed is void unless the other spouse joins. A joint tenancy with survivorship is severed and becomes a tenancy in common. Once such a deed is recorded, IC 32-21-1-15(b) voids any later conveyance of the property that was not recorded before the owner's death. Owners who may sell later should look at the county records before they act.

Transfer on death deed versus quitclaim

Deeding a house while a tax sale redemption period is running brings in a special rule. IC 32-21-8-7 keeps the auditor from endorsing the conveyance until the buyer has paid the county treasurer the full amount needed to redeem under IC 6-1.1-25 and has shown written proof. Unless the deed is recorded before the redemption period ends, it is void.

A quitclaim does not skip any step here. The treasurer is paid, the auditor endorses and the recorder files, in that order, while the one-year redemption period for ordinary tax sales keeps running.

If you are the grantor and a redemption deadline is close, call the county treasurer first for the payoff figure, because the other two offices cannot act until that payment is shown.

Property in a tax sale redemption period

Deeding a house during a tax sale redemption period triggers a special rule. Under IC 32-21-8-7, the auditor cannot endorse the conveyance until the buyer has paid the county treasurer the full redemption amount under IC 6-1.1-25 and shown written proof. The conveyance is also void unless it is recorded by the end of the redemption period.

A quitclaim in that situation is no shortcut. The treasurer's payoff, the auditor's endorsement and the recorder's filing all have to happen in order, and the one-year redemption period for ordinary tax sales runs on its own clock.

Selling a house after a quitclaim transfer

A cash buyer still needs the chain of title to hold together, so a recent quitclaim among family members raises questions a title company will ask. Who signed, whether all owners joined, whether the deed was recorded and whether a sales disclosure form went in with it are the points that decide how fast a closing moves.

Recent quitclaims also affect property tax benefits. The homestead deduction is tied to the owner's principal residence, and current rules add a 10 percent penalty for keeping a deduction after ineligibility. An owner who stops living in a house after deeding it should notify the county auditor.

Before you list, pull the recorded deed and confirm the names match your ID and the tax bill. A mismatch is easy to fix before an offer and slow to fix after one.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed legal in Indiana?

Yes. IC 32-21-1-15 recognizes a conveyance worded in substance as 'A.B. quitclaims to C.D.' if it describes the property, states the consideration and is signed, sealed and acknowledged.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed?

The recorder charges $25 for an ordinary deed under IC 36-2-7-10, with a $25 plus $5 per extra page schedule for oversized pages. A sales disclosure form adds a $20 fee paid to the county auditor when the transfer is for value.

Does a quitclaim deed need a notary?

Yes. IC 32-21-2-3 requires an acknowledgment or a proof, and Indiana allows a remote notary under the cited statutes.

Do I need a sales disclosure form for a quitclaim deed?

Not always. Quitclaim deeds that do not serve as a source of title, and gifts with no valuable consideration, are exempt. A transfer for valuable consideration does need one.

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. It passes only the interest the grantor has under IC 32-17-2-2, and the short statutory form contains no title promises.

What a transfer on death deed is

A transfer on death (TOD) deed passes real estate to a named beneficiary when the owner dies, without a probate transfer for that parcel. Indiana allows it under the Transfer on Death Property Act, IC 32-17-14, with the real estate rules in section 11.

You keep the house for life. The beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation until you die, and if you sell, the designation ends.

The deed works when the owner, or the owner's legal representative, signs it and it is recorded with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits, before the owner dies.

What makes a TOD deed valid

The big requirement is recording while the owner is alive. A TOD deed that is not recorded before death is void.

  • No payment is required for the transfer.
  • The deed does not have to be delivered to the beneficiary.
  • The county auditor's endorsement is not needed to record it.
  • The beneficiary can be a revocable or an irrevocable trust.
  • The wording can be, in substance, a conveyance "TOD to" the beneficiary.

In practice, the steps are short. Confirm how title is held, have the deed prepared, sign it, and take it to the county recorder where the parcel sits. Then keep the recorded copy with your papers and tell the beneficiary where it is, even though delivery is not required. If the recorder never receives the deed before you die, it does nothing.

Since delivery is not required, a beneficiary may find out about the deed only after the owner dies. A family that suspects one exists can search the county recorder's records for the parcel.

How the form of ownership changes a TOD deed

What the deed does depends on how the owner holds title, and some forms call for extra care. Section 11 spells out the results.

Form of ownershipEffect of a TOD deed
Tenancy by the entiretyVoid unless the other spouse joins
Joint tenancy with survivorshipSevers the joint tenancy; co-owners become tenants in common
Tenancy in commonThe owner's interest passes to the beneficiary
Life estate measured by the owner's lifeThe conveyance is void

Married couples who own together should not assume one spouse can sign alone. Questions like these are a good reason to have an attorney review a recorded deed.

Changing or revoking a TOD deed

You record a later document in the county while you are alive. IC 32-17-14-16 lets the owner revoke or change the designation by recording a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit that does so. An unrecorded document is void.

Informal fixes do not work:

  • Writing on a recorded TOD deed or destroying a copy has no effect on the designation.
  • A will or trust cannot revoke or modify a TOD deed.
  • A newer designation replaces an earlier one unless it says otherwise.

For joint tenants with survivorship, a change needs the agreement of each living owner. For tenants by the entirety, both spouses must agree while both are alive.

Selling the house after you sign a TOD deed

A sale cancels the TOD for that property. Under section 16, transferring your interest during life, with or without payment, ends the beneficiary designation. A real estate deed given this way is void unless it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

So an owner with a TOD deed on record can still sell to a cash buyer. The buyer's title company searches the record, finds the TOD deed and confirms the owner's right to convey. The beneficiary has no rights in the home while the owner is alive.

Families under pressure should know this. A beneficiary cannot block a sale by the living owner, and an owner who needs to move can sell on their own schedule.

Liens and creditors

A TOD deed does not shield the house. The beneficiary takes the property subject to the liens and security interests that exist (IC 32-17-14-19). A mortgage, a recorded easement or a judgment lien stays on the house after the transfer.

Creditors keep their rights too. IC 32-17-14-29 says the chapter does not limit what an owner's creditors can do against beneficiaries and other transferees. A beneficiary's liability for creditor claims and statutory allowances is set in IC 32-17-13.

Unpaid property tax is a lien that follows the house. Our Indiana tax lien guide explains how it works. A beneficiary who inherits a house with delinquent tax inherits the tax bill with it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Indiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can a beneficiary sell after the owner dies?

Yes. Once the beneficiary holds title through the recorded deed, the house is theirs to sell.

A beneficiary should take these steps:

  • Get a certified death certificate.
  • Ask the title company to pull the recorded TOD deed and any later revocation.
  • Check for a mortgage, tax due or liens.
  • See an attorney if a spouse, children or other heirs may have claims. IC 32-17-14-25 covers the rights of surviving spouses and children.

A house in poor repair can still be sold as is. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on inherited Indiana homes without requiring repairs, and a cash closing skips the listing, showings and buyer financing delays.

Other parts of the Transfer on Death Property Act

The act reaches well beyond deeds. The same chapter governs designations on accounts, tangible personal property and registrations in beneficiary form, so a family may be sorting out several transfers at once.

  • Section 20 requires a beneficiary to survive the owner, and section 22 covers substitution for beneficiaries who do not survive.
  • Section 23 deals with the effect of dissolution or annulment of a marriage.
  • Section 24 deals with fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake and lack of capacity.
  • Section 17 deals with the powers of an attorney in fact, a guardian, a conservator or an agent.
  • Section 32 deals with out-of-state beneficiary designations.

Each has its own conditions. If a family member signed a deed while ill, or a divorce came after the deed was recorded, an attorney will start with those sections.

When a TOD deed is the wrong tool

It fits best with a single parcel and one clear beneficiary. It fits poorly when several heirs may disagree, when the home carries heavy debt, or when the owner wants a trust to manage the property.

  • A beneficiary who dies before the owner brings in the survival and substitution rules in sections 20 and 22.
  • Co-owners can undo the intended result by how they hold title.
  • The deed does not remove debts from the property.

An estate planning attorney can compare a TOD deed with a trust or a will for your situation. This page is general information and is not legal advice.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does an Indiana TOD deed avoid probate?

For the parcel it covers, yes. The beneficiary takes title through the recorded deed. Other assets in the estate can still need probate.

Where do you record an Indiana TOD deed?

With the recorder of deeds in the county where the real estate is located, before the owner's death. A deed recorded after death is void.

Can I cancel a TOD deed by writing a new will?

No. A will or trust cannot revoke or modify a TOD deed. The owner must record a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit before death.

Can the beneficiary stop me from selling my house?

No. While the owner is alive, a beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation. A sale during life ends the designation for that parcel.

Does the beneficiary have to pay my mortgage?

The beneficiary takes the house subject to existing liens and security interests. The loan stays attached to the property, and lenders keep their rights.

How an Indiana property tax lien works

Indiana's property tax lien is created by statute and sits on the land itself. IC 6-1.1-22-13 puts every parcel of real estate under a lien for its levied taxes, along with any penalties and costs.

It attaches on the assessment date for the tax year. A sale or transfer does not erase it. List a house with a year of tax unpaid and the lien stays on the parcel until somebody pays, so the title company deals with it when you close.

The same law ranks it above every other lien. Mortgages, judgment liens and contractor claims all come after it. It lasts ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due, and that period can stretch if the county starts enforcement inside it.

When Indiana property tax becomes delinquent

An installment goes delinquent the day after it is missed. Under IC 6-1.1-22-9, a year's tax is generally split into two equal payments, due May 10 and November 10 of the following year. A weekend or holiday pushes the deadline to the next business day. The state's Department of Local Government Finance keeps a due dates page with the current schedule.

Your payment is timely if it arrives, carries a postmark, or goes out by electronic transfer on or before the deadline (IC 6-1.1-37-10). Once an installment is late, penalties start right away.

Late payment penalties

The first penalty is either 5 percent or 10 percent of the delinquent amount. The 5 percent rate applies when a real property installment is paid in full within 30 days of the due date and the owner has no earlier delinquency on that parcel. Every other late payment is charged 10 percent. Marion County describes it the same way: pay within 30 days with no back taxes and the penalty is 5 percent, and after that it is 10 percent.

Later years add more. In each following year, another 10 percent applies to unpaid tax on the day after each installment due date. Those later penalties land on the unpaid principal only, so a penalty does not compound on an earlier penalty.

Late payment situationPenalty added
Paid within 30 days, no earlier delinquency on the parcel5% of the delinquent amount
Any other late payment10% of the amount due
Still unpaid after each later installment dateAdditional 10% on unpaid principal

What happens when the tax stays unpaid

The county can eventually put the parcel into a tax sale, which is the main way a tax lien turns into a change of ownership. A taxing unit can also sue the person liable and recover the tax, penalties and collection costs, including reasonable attorney fees and court costs.

Counties take the steps in order:

  • The county auditor builds a delinquency list and a notice of sale.
  • The county treasurer and auditor ask the court for a judgment and an order of sale.
  • The property is offered at a public auction, subject to redemption.
  • The owner gets a redemption window before a buyer can ask for a tax deed.

Our Indiana tax sale page covers the auction and the redemption window in detail. This page stays on the lien and on clearing it.

Can you set up a payment plan on delinquent taxes?

Yes, the law contemplates one. IC 6-1.1-24-1.2 covers removing a property from the delinquency list and arranging to pay delinquent taxes. Each county sets its own terms, so ask your treasurer what it will take.

Marion County treats a tax sale payment plan and partial payments as separate topics on its Stop a Tax Sale page. The Treasurer's Office is at (317) 327-4444 or mytaxes@indy.gov. Behind on a plan? Call before a sale date is set.

A plan has limits if you plan to sell. The lien remains until the tax is paid in full, and a buyer's title company will still want a payoff at closing.

State tax warrants

Unpaid state tax can also become a lien on your house, in whichever county the warrant is recorded. This one is separate from the property tax lien. After a demand notice goes unanswered for 20 days, the Department of State Revenue can issue a tax warrant, and a 10 percent collection fee is added to the unpaid tax (IC 6-8.1-8-2).

The circuit court clerk records the warrant as a judgment against the taxpayer, and that judgment gives the state a lien on the taxpayer's real and personal property interests there. A filed judgment is valid for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10 year periods.

The two liens differ in timing. The property tax lien attaches on the assessment date and ranks above every other lien. The warrant lien attaches when the clerk records the judgment, and it reaches only the county where it was recorded.

A taxpayer can ask for a release once the debt is satisfied, and the department must release a warrant issued in error. Ask your title company to run a search so any warrant shows up before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Indiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Vacant and abandoned property sales

A few delinquent parcels never go through the regular sale, and their owners get no redemption right. IC 6-1.1-24-1.5 lets a county, city or town executive certify a delinquent property that a court or hearing authority found vacant or abandoned. The auditor then sells it at auction, and the owner cannot redeem after the sale date.

The minimum bid on those parcels equals the property's share of the county's actual sale costs, not the full tax debt. A vacant house with years of unpaid tax is exactly what this rule targets.

  • The tax must be delinquent from the prior year's fall installment or earlier.
  • A court or hearing authority must find the property vacant or abandoned.
  • The auditor publishes the sale notice at least 30 days before the sale.

Tax liens in Marion County (Indianapolis)

Marion County places a tax lien on homes with unpaid property taxes and sells those liens at an online auction each year. Registered bidders put down a $2,500 deposit for the regular portion of the sale.

To stop a scheduled sale, an owner pays all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 tax sale administration fee. The cutoff is 4:30 p.m. on a day shortly before the sale, and payment is limited to cash, certified check, cashier's check or money order.

Marion County Treasurer: City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis, IN 46204. Auditor: Suite W-125, phone 317.327.4646.

Clearing a lien before closing

Most sellers never write a check for the lien. Closing pays it: the title agent requests a payoff from the county treasurer and sends the money from your proceeds.

Do these four things early:

  • Get the current tax bill and a payoff number with penalties included.
  • Search for a state tax warrant filed under your name.
  • Find out if the parcel sits on a delinquency list or already has a sale date.
  • With a sale date close, ask the treasurer what time payment is due and what forms of payment it takes.

Cash Home Buyers can purchase a house carrying these liens and coordinate with the title company so the unpaid tax is paid out of what you receive. A cash sale skips repairs and showings. You can ask for an offer without fixing a thing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long does a property tax lien last in Indiana?

Ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due. If the county starts enforcement inside that period, the deadline can extend as needed to finish it.

Can I sell my house with a tax lien in Indiana?

Yes. The lien follows the property, so the unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. A title company confirms the payoff amount before the deed is recorded.

Does a tax lien rank ahead of my mortgage?

Yes. IC 6-1.1-22-13 makes the property tax lien superior to all other liens, so it is paid before a mortgage in a forced sale.

What is the penalty for paying Indiana property tax late?

Five percent if you pay within 30 days and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel, and ten percent in any other case. Another 10 percent applies to unpaid principal after each later due date.

Who do I call in Indianapolis about delinquent property tax?

Call the Marion County Treasurer's Office at (317) 327-4444 for balances and payments. The Auditor's Office at 317.327.4646 handles tax sale questions.

How Indiana taxes the profit on a house

Hoosier sellers face no standalone levy on property gains. Profit from a house is folded into ordinary income under the individual adjusted gross income tax. The calculation begins with your federal adjusted gross income (the Section 62 definition) and then runs through Indiana's own additions and subtractions. A taxable gain on your federal return therefore shows up on the state return too.

The state rate is 2.95 percent for 2026, stepping down to 2.90 percent for 2027. One flat rate covers all of your income, gain included.

Counties layer a local income tax over the state rate. Howard County, as one example, sits at 0.0235, or 2.35 percent, for periods starting October 1, 2026. Where you lived on January 1 fixes which county rate applies to you, and counties can adjust rates in January and October. The IT-40 booklet prints each county's current figure.

Who qualifies for the federal exclusion

For most owners, this federal break settles whether any profit ever reaches the Indiana calculation. One seller filing alone can shield up to $250,000 of gain from the sale of a main home. A married couple on a joint return can shield up to $500,000.

You must pass two tests, each looking back across the 5 years that end on your closing date:

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for at least 24 months of that window.
  • Use: the house was your home for at least 24 months of that window. On a joint return, each spouse has to pass this test.
  • The two 24-month stretches do not have to overlap.
  • A separate limit: if you claimed the exclusion on a different home sale within the previous two years, you cannot claim it again.

A lender or title company that issues a Form 1099-S triggers a reporting duty, so the sale goes on your return even when every dollar of gain is excluded. If part of the gain is taxable, you will also file Schedule D and Form 8949. Someone on qualified official extended duty may elect to pause the five-year clock for as long as ten years.

Federal rates on gain above the exclusion

A house held for more than a year produces long-term gain, which falls into 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on your taxable income. Anything held a year or less counts as short-term and is taxed like wages. The brackets below are the 2025 figures. They shift every year, so look up the current ones before you file.

Filing status0 percent up to15 percent up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

Taxable income above the 15 percent range moves to 20 percent. The part of a gain tied to past depreciation (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) tops out at 25 percent. Higher earners can also owe the net investment income tax. If you sell your own home at a loss, the loss cannot be deducted.

Which Indiana adjustments matter to a seller?

Start with the order of operations. First decide how much of the gain the federal exclusion removes. Whatever remains lands in federal adjusted gross income, and only then do Indiana's adjustments apply. Most sellers who qualify for the full exclusion never reach the second step.

The handiest adjustment is a subtraction for property tax paid on a principal residence, capped at $2,500 ($1,250 for separate filers). It appears in the statute alongside subtractions for Social Security benefits and some military income.

The same statute lists additions as well, including state income tax deducted on the federal return and certain bonus depreciation and Section 179 amounts. If you ever depreciated the house as a rental, go through that list line by line with a preparer.

Limits can move between legislative sessions. Read the amount in the current Indiana tax booklet before you count on it.

Selling a house you inherited

When an heir sells, the taxable gain is measured from a stepped-up starting value. That usually leaves much less profit on paper than the original owner's purchase price would suggest. Basis equals the fair market value on the date of death, or the value on the alternate valuation date when the estate's personal representative chooses that route.

There is one trap. If you or your spouse handed appreciated property to the decedent within a year of death, the basis reverts to the decedent's adjusted basis from just before death. Hold on to the appraisal or the estate's valuation, because it becomes your cost figure at filing time.

Heirs who sell soon after the death often find the sale price barely above the date-of-death value, which leaves little or no gain to report. Waiting a long time before selling lets gain build on the estate's or the heir's side.

Indiana repealed its inheritance tax, and probate decides who may sign the deed. The estate tax and probate pages on this site cover those steps.

Rental and investment houses

The exclusion is written for a main home, so a rental normally produces taxable gain. The federal side taxes the depreciation-recapture portion at no more than 25 percent.

Indiana then applies its own rate to the federal figure after state modifications. What you owe in total depends on three things: your federal bracket, your county rate and whether any part of the gain qualifies for the exclusion.

Owners of a rental who plan to sell should also decide early whether the tenant stays through closing, since a buyer who wants to move in will price the house differently from one who wants rent.

A tenant in the house adds a second set of questions about notice and timing. The Indiana eviction process page walks through them.

Paperwork to gather before you talk to a preparer

A preparer can give you a useful estimate in one sitting when the records are ready. Pull together:

  • The closing statement from your purchase, plus receipts for capital improvements
  • The dates you moved in and out, so the 24-month tests can be checked
  • Details of any earlier home sale where you took the exclusion
  • The date of death and the valuation, if the house came to you by inheritance
  • Depreciation schedules, if the house was ever rented
  • Your county of residence on January 1

Selling fast for cash does not alter any of this. The tax follows your basis, your years in the home and your January 1 address, so the records count for more than the identity of the buyer. A cash sale also skips lender underwriting, so the stretch between contract and closing can be short. Collect the records before you list, not after.

Frequently asked questions

What does Indiana charge on profit from a home sale?

Profit flows through the state's individual adjusted gross income tax, currently 2.95 percent for 2026 and dropping to 2.90 percent for 2027. Your county then adds a local income tax.

Is gain covered by the federal exclusion taxed by Indiana?

Generally no. The state return begins with federal adjusted gross income, which leaves out gain you excluded. State additions can alter the picture, so a preparer should read your return.

What is the largest gain a seller can exclude?

A seller filing alone can exclude $250,000, and spouses filing together can exclude $500,000. Both need to pass the ownership and residence tests across 24 of the prior 60 months, with no other exclusion claimed in the last two years.

Does an heir owe tax measured from what the owner originally paid?

No, the starting value is the market value on the date of death. A gift of appreciated property to the decedent in the year before death changes that rule.

Must I report a sale that produced no taxable gain?

If a Form 1099-S arrives, yes. Schedule D and Form 8949 enter the picture only when some of the profit is taxable.

How an Indiana tax sale works

A tax sale is a public auction of a parcel with delinquent taxes, and the sale stays subject to redemption. The county auditor publishes a notice of eligible properties. The auditor and treasurer then apply to the court for a judgment and an order of sale (IC 6-1.1-24-2).

The notice names the owner (or at least one owner), the parcel key number and street address, and the sale place, dates and times. An online sale must say so and explain how to take part. To fight the judgment, an owner files a defense with the court and serves the auditor and treasurer before the earliest application date in the notice. The court sets a hearing at least seven days before the advertised sale.

Bidders are not buying your house outright. They are buying the county's lien, and you can still pay to take the property back during the redemption period.

Minimum bid

No parcel sells for less than the minimum bid, which is the delinquent tax plus the cost of running the sale. Five pieces make up that figure.

  • Delinquent taxes and special assessments.
  • Taxes and assessments due in the sale year, delinquent or not.
  • Penalties on the delinquencies.
  • An auditor fee equal to the greater of $25 or postage and publication costs, plus other actual costs tied to the sale.
  • Unpaid costs from a prior tax sale.

A bidder can go higher. The amount above the minimum is the overbid, and it can turn into surplus for the owner, covered further down.

How long do you have to redeem?

Most owners get one year from the date of sale to redeem. If the property went to a qualified purchasing agency, the period is 120 days (IC 6-1.1-25-4).

A few situations change the clock:

  • Property on the county's vacant and abandoned list has no right to redeem.
  • If the county acquires a lien that is not sold as a certificate, redemption runs 120 days from the day the lien is acquired.
  • A parcel that was offered but did not sell gets 120 days from the end of the sale.

Marion County gives the same two main periods on its redemption amount page: one year from the sale date for a sold parcel, 120 days for a parcel that was offered but did not sell.

The treasurer and an owner can also agree in writing to extend redemption by one year, as long as the owner pays the full redemption amount before the extended period ends. If the owner breaks the agreement, the treasurer can end it with 30 days' written notice.

What redemption costs

The redemption amount has several parts (IC 6-1.1-25-2). The base is 110 percent of the minimum bid if you redeem within six months of the sale, or 115 percent if you redeem after six months but inside the year.

Cost componentHow it is figured
Base amount110% of minimum bid within 6 months; 115% after that
OverbidAmount the price exceeded the minimum bid, plus 5% per year (sales after June 30, 2014)
Taxes the buyer paid after the saleReimbursed with 5% per year interest (sales after June 30, 2014)
Certified costsAttorney fees, notice costs and title search costs, certified to the auditor
New delinquenciesTaxes, penalties and fees that became delinquent after the sale

The base percentage jumps after month six, so redeeming early costs less. Ask the treasurer for a written redemption figure before you send money, since it changes with the date.

What a tax deed does to your title

When nobody redeems, the buyer can petition for a tax deed, and that deed ends your interest in the house. Under IC 6-1.1-25-4 it conveys a fee simple absolute, free of most liens. Recorded easements and governmental police powers are among the exceptions.

The deed has its own deadline. The auditor cannot issue or record it unless, within 150 days after the court hearing that grants the buyer's petition, the court order and sales disclosure form are filed, recording fees are paid, and all outstanding property taxes are paid.

After a sale, the path left to an owner is short and expensive. Redeem or sell before the deed issues.

Surplus money after the sale

If a parcel sells above the minimum bid and nobody redeems, the former owner of record may be owed the surplus (IC 6-1.1-24-7).

The buyer's payment goes first to taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, then to other delinquent taxes. Whatever is left goes into a tax sale surplus fund.

  • The owner of record may file a verified claim for the surplus.
  • If the auditor and treasurer approve, the auditor issues a warrant for the amount due.
  • Surplus not claimed within three years after receipt goes to the county general fund.

A claim made through a contract holder, executor, attorney in fact or guardian goes through the court, and a court may direct payment only within three years after the sale. Indiana also limits agreements for recovering surplus money, and the attorney general enforces those limits.

How Marion County runs its tax sale

Marion County holds an online tax lien sale every fall over four days, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The non-profit portion runs first, then the regular portion, and parcels are auctioned in numeric order without a break between townships.

Bidders for the regular portion post a $2,500 deposit and must register a few days ahead. New bidders without evidence of credit from a bank are approved for $100,000 as individuals or $250,000 as companies.

Marion is a consolidated city county, so its surplus rule is different. The treasurer may pay taxes that come due during the redemption period out of the surplus held in the owner's name.

You can check whether your parcel sold with the sold parcel finder. Tax sale questions go to the Auditor at MCATaxSale@indy.gov.

Stopping a Marion County tax sale

Pay everything owed before the cutoff. That means all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 administration fee, due by 4:30 p.m. on the posted day shortly before the sale.

On auction day the Treasurer collects payment after 8 a.m. in room 1001 of the City-County Building. Personal and business checks are refused.

Selling first is another way out. If a buyer closes before the auction, the title company pays the tax out of the proceeds and the parcel never reaches the sale. Already got a notice? Call (317) 327-4444 to confirm what you owe.

What to weigh before the sale date

Three things drive the decision: timing, money, and the shape the house is in.

  • Get the redemption figure first, because it rises after six months.
  • Ask whether the parcel is on the vacant and abandoned list, where no redemption exists.
  • Work out whether the home has equity above the tax debt. If it does, selling protects that equity.
  • Keep copies of every notice you receive.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is, including ones facing a tax sale, with no repairs or cleanup needed. We can go through the numbers with you and the title company.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can I still redeem my Indiana house after the tax sale?

Yes, in most cases. You generally have one year from the date of sale, or 120 days if the property sold to a qualified purchasing agency. Parcels on the vacant and abandoned list have no redemption right.

What is the redemption percentage in Indiana?

It is 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months of the sale and 115 percent after six months but inside the year. Other costs and interest are added on top.

Who buys at an Indiana tax sale?

Registered bidders. In Marion County, bidders for the regular portion post a $2,500 deposit and register before the sale.

Can I get the surplus if my house sold above the minimum bid?

Possibly. If the property is not redeemed, the owner of record may file a verified claim. Unclaimed surplus goes to the county general fund after three years.

Can I sell my house before it goes to tax sale?

Yes. A sale that closes before the auction lets the title company pay the tax debt from the proceeds. Confirm the payoff amount and the sale date with the county first.

How a sheriff sale works

A sheriff sale is the public auction that follows a court judgment of foreclosure, and the county sheriff conducts it. Indiana foreclosures go through a judge, so the sale arrives late in a chain of notices, filings and waiting periods.

The governing rules are in IC 32-29-7. The sheriff must sell in a way 'reasonably likely to bring the highest net proceeds' after expenses. A judge can order an auctioneer when that is economically feasible or when all creditors agree, and the sheriff then has 14 days from the order to engage one.

Sales may run between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on any day except Sunday. The sheriff can hold one electronically, at the sheriff's office, or at another location likely to draw higher bids.

Timeline from missed payments to the sale

The statutes set minimum gaps between steps. These are the ones that apply to a typical owner-occupied home.

StepTiming
Presuit notice by certified mail (IC 32-30-10.5-8)At least 30 days before the lender files
Request a settlement conferenceWithin 30 days after the complaint is served
Process on a judgment may issue (IC 32-29-7-3)Not until 3 months after the complaint is filed
Lender files the praecipeGenerally within 180 days
Sheriff schedules the saleWithin 120 days after certification (60 days for judgments on abandoned property)
Newspaper noticeOnce a week for 3 weeks; first notice at least 30 days before the sale

The lender pays an administrative fee of up to $300 when it files the praecipe. At the first publication the sheriff also serves written notice on each owner, for a fee of $10 for one owner and $3 for each additional one. Notices go up at the courthouse door as well. If the sale is canceled, the sheriff must tell each owner in writing.

Options before the sale

A homeowner has several moves available before the auction, from a settlement conference to paying off the judgment.

  • Request a settlement conference. For an owner-occupied home, the court mails a notice of the right to one, and the owner must ask within 30 days after service of the complaint. If the owner asks, the judge cannot sign the foreclosure order until the conference has taken place, and the lender must send a representative.
  • Call the foreclosure hotline. The Indiana Foreclosure Prevention Network answers at 877-438-4673 (877-GET-HOPE) and can connect a homeowner with a pro bono attorney for the conference.
  • Redeem before the sale. Under IC 32-29-7-7, any owner or part owner can pay the judgment plus interest and costs before the sale. The money goes to the clerk if the decree has not yet been issued to the sheriff, and to the sheriff after that. Once the property is redeemed, the sale cannot proceed and the order of sale is vacated.
  • Stay put. IC 32-29-7-11 lets an owner who lives in the property keep possession rent free until the foreclosure sale, provided the court finds no waste or damage. An owner who stops paying taxes may keep only the part used as a dwelling, up to fifteen acres.

A part owner who redeems gets a lien on the other owners' shares for their portion, bearing 8 percent annual interest plus costs. Heirs who share a house and disagree about paying should know this rule.

What happens on sale day

Details vary by county. In Grant County, sales are held at 10:00 a.m. at the Sheriff's Department in Marion. Bidders must submit a handwritten bid form before that hour, and there is no minimum bid.

The winning bidder must pay in full by 3:00 p.m. that day, or the sale is voided and the next highest bidder is notified. The dollar figure on the sale list is the judgment owed when the paperwork was filed, which may not match what the bank will bid. The bank is always represented, by fax or in person. The office has no keys, does not show properties and has no information about them. If a house is occupied, the sheriff will evict the occupants within 24 hours.

Bidders face a legal check as well. IC 32-29-7-4.6, added by a 2022 law, requires each bidder to sign a sworn statement that they owe no delinquent property taxes, no unpaid judgments to a local government and no building code penalties, and that they are not bidding for someone barred from the sale. Giving false information is a Level 6 felony. IC 32-29-7-9 bars the sheriff from buying at the sale.

Taxes and liens that must be paid first

The side that requested the sale pays delinquent real estate taxes first. Under IC 32-29-7-8.5, the party that filed the praecipe must pay delinquent property taxes, sewer liens, special assessments, penalties and interest due on the sale date, or the amount needed to redeem if a tax sale certificate is outstanding. If those payments are not made in full by the sale date, the sheriff must cancel the sale, and a new sale needs a fresh praecipe, costs and re-advertising.

What the buyer receives and where leftover money goes

The sheriff prepares a deed and delivers it to the buyer right after the sale, then files it with the county recorder unless the foreclosed mortgage was HUD-insured. The deed must be sufficient to pass the full interest of every party to the suit and anyone claiming under them. The sheriff then files a return with the clerk.

Sale money follows a set order under IC 32-30-10-14. Expenses of the offer and sale come first, then principal, interest and costs, then the remaining secured balance not yet due. Anything left goes to the clerk, and the court directs it to the mortgage debtor, the debtor's heirs, or others the debtor assigned to.

Allen County has put numbers on this. A court program launched in 2021 found 45 former owners with a combined $282,000 in unclaimed surplus, with individual amounts ranging from under $200 to nearly $50,000. Claims are made by letter to the clerk with the original case number, a court order is needed to release the money, and unclaimed funds can move to the Indiana Attorney General's Unclaimed Property Division after five years.
